Spherical geometry in stereographic and gnomonic charts

Source: R/layers-spherical-geometry.R
coord_spherical_geometry_3d.Rd

Maps the unit three-sphere in four dimensions to three display coordinates. Paths and faces follow shorter great circles through the shared sampler. Ambient inputs map x, y, z and w. Stereographic input is the inverse chart (2p, |p|^2-1)/(1+|p|^2). The display map is X[1:3]/(1-X[4]). Gnomonic coordinates are the homogeneous point X itself, (X1:3, X4), read in oriented projective space (Stolfi 1991): X and -X are distinct points, so the chart covers the whole sphere, and the display X[1:3]/X[4] shows the hemisphere X4 > 0. Great circles are straight lines and totally geodesic faces are planar, so SO(4) acts linearly. Stereographic coordinates are homogeneous, (X1:3, 1 - X4), so the pole is the point at infinity and box clipping happens before division. Paths are clipped analytically on their great circles against the box planes, which are planes of R^4. Faces are sampled only outside a cap around the pole whose image lies outside twice the box circumradius, and the scene engine clips their triangles to the box in homogeneous coordinates, so fibres and faces through the pole are drawn up to the panel box.

Usage

coord_spherical_geometry_3d(
  dim = 3,
  model = c("stereographic", "gnomonic"),
  input = model,
  extent = 3,
  inside = FALSE,
  observer = NULL,
  fog = NULL,
  ...
)

Arguments

dim

Spherical dimension, currently three.

model, input

Display model and input chart.

extent

Positive half-width of the finite display box. Gnomonic geometry is clipped to the finite box of the hemisphere in front of the observer.

inside

Use a first-person perspective eye at the gnomonic origin.

observer

Observer point in the input chart, an ambient unit four-vector, or an SO(4) matrix taking the observer to the origin.

fog

Optional positive inverse-area brightness scale. At each primitive centre brightness is min(1, fog/sin(d)^2), in linear light.

...

Arguments to coord_3d(), including SO(4) isometry matrices from rotate_4d(). These also work in animate_3d(isometry=).

Value

A Coord3D object.

Details

In the gnomonic model an observer or isometry is an SO(4) matrix acting on the homogeneous coordinates (X1:3, X4), carried by the camera pre-transform as in Weeks (2002). The geometry of the whole sphere is emitted once, with packet vertices of either sign of w; the scene engine applies the action and clips in homogeneous coordinates to w >= 0 and the panel box (Blinn and Newell 1978), so the hemisphere within a quarter turn of the observer is drawn and a rotation brings the far hemisphere into view. animate_3d(isometry = ) frames, such as Clifford translations from rotate_4d() with left or right quaternions, only recompile. Inside views restrict geometry to the observer hemisphere and finite panel box. Near defaults to sqrt(machine epsilon), and far to the farthest panel-box corner, in normalised camera units. Azimuth, elevation and roll set facing. The stereographic model applies the action before packing.

References

Johnson (2011). A visualization of the Hopf fibration. https://nilesjohnson.net/hopf.html. Obermeyer. Jenn3d. https://jenn3d.org/. Weeks (2002). Real-time rendering in curved spaces. doi:10.1109/MCG.2002.1046633 . Coulon et al. (2022), Section 7. https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.15801. Stolfi (1991). Oriented projective geometry. Academic Press. Hart, Francis and Kauffman (1994). Visualizing quaternion rotation. doi:10.1145/195784.197480 .

Examples

d <- data.frame(x=c(-1,1),y=.4,z=0)
ggplot2::ggplot(d,ggplot2::aes(x,y,z=z))+geom_path_3d()+
  coord_spherical_geometry_3d(isometry=rotate_4d("xw",.2))
d <- data.frame(x=.5,y=c(-.2,.2,.2,-.2),z=c(-.2,-.2,.2,.2))
ggplot2::ggplot(d,ggplot2::aes(x,y,z=z))+geom_polygon_3d(fill="steelblue")+
  coord_spherical_geometry_3d(inside=TRUE,azimuth=180,elevation=0,fog=.1)
